evidence: M-O s.v. class: academic career (cursus acadēmicus); s.v. graduate (gradus acadēmicus)
terms.comment: Classically “of the Academy”, Plato’s school: Cicero’s Acadēmica, and acadēmicus, an Academic philosopher (Lewis & Short). The university sense is modern.

terms.gloss: of the schools; scholarly, academic (as against public life); (as a noun) a schoolman
terms.comment: Post-Augustan: of the schools of rhetoric. Pliny uses it of a man who lives for study rather than for the courts, “academic” in that sense, often with a smile (scholasticā lēge, by the rules of the schools, Ep. 2.20.9).
The plain word for a scholar or a scholarly book: vir doctus, a learned man.

phrases.latin: Scholasticīs porrō dominīs, ut hic est, sufficit abundē tantum solī, ut relevāre caput, reficere oculōs, reptāre per līmitem ūnamque sēmitam terere omnēsque vīteculās suās nōsse et numerāre arbusculās possint.
phrases.english: For academic owners like him, just enough land is plenty: enough to rest the head and the eyes, stroll along the boundary, wear down a single path, know every one of their vines and count their little trees.

phrases.latin: Annum sexāgēnsimum excessit et adhūc scholasticus tantum est
phrases.english: He is past sixty and still nothing but an academic

sources: Lewis & Short: academicus · Lewis & Short: scholasticus · Lewis & Short: doctus
